prompt: In many countries people are having their first child at a much later age than previous generations did. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this development.
essay:
The average age at which people have a first child has risen sharply in a single generation. The change brings real benefits to the individuals making the choice, while most of its costs are either medical or demographic, and the second kind is easy to ignore because it arrives late.

For the parents, the advantages are concrete. A couple in their mid-thirties are likely to have settled housing, established incomes and some understanding of what they are undertaking, none of which is typical at twenty-two. For women in particular, delay protects a career at exactly the point where seniority is decided; a parent who returns from leave with an established position loses far less than one who never had it. There is reasonable evidence, too, that children of older parents do well educationally, which is presumably a function of household resources rather than of age itself.

The disadvantages fall into two categories. The first is straightforwardly biological: fertility declines with age, treatment is expensive and often unsuccessful, and both maternal and neonatal risks rise. Some couples who delay do not end up with the family they planned. The second is collective. If a whole society postpones, birth rates fall below replacement, and a shrinking working-age population is left supporting a growing retired one. Individually rational timing produces a collectively awkward result.

On balance the development seems to me positive for the people making the decision and difficult for the societies they live in. That is not a reason to advise anyone to have children earlier, but it is a reason to make having them earlier less costly than it currently is. Governments that treat the trend purely as a private choice are therefore missing half of it.
title: Starting a family later
